# Measuring Performance

The README of `foks-rs` publishes three latency numbers. This chapter is
about what those numbers mean, how they were produced, and why the
methodology behind them is more interesting than the numbers themselves.
Along the way it introduces three ideas from the practice of latency
measurement that any reader who benchmarks software should know:
percentiles, warmup, and coordinated omission.

## Why not the average

Suppose a desktop application makes a history request to its local agent
every half second, and the developer wants to know whether a new
background feature has made the foreground slower. The average latency is
almost useless for this. A feature that makes one request in fifty take a
full second while leaving the rest untouched barely moves the mean, yet the
user notices every one of those slow requests. What the user experiences is
the *tail* of the distribution.

A *percentile* is the value below which a given fraction of observations
fall. The 95th percentile (p95) is the latency that 95% of requests beat;
one request in twenty is slower. Percentiles are order statistics: they
are computed by sorting the observations and indexing, and they are robust
to a handful of extreme outliers in a way the mean is not. Dean and
Barroso's *The Tail at Scale* explains why tails matter more as systems
grow: a user-facing operation that touches many components sees the
*worst* of them, so the fraction of slow operations compounds.

The benchmark harness computes p95 by sorting the recorded durations and
taking the element at index ⌊0.95 × n⌋.

## Warmup and coordinated omission

Two systematic errors are easy to make.

*Warmup.* The first seconds of any process are unrepresentative: caches
are cold, just-in-time compilers have not compiled hot paths, connection
pools are empty, and the operating system has not paged the binary in.
Including them in a measurement biases it toward slowness in a way that
has nothing to do with the code under test. The remedy is to run the
workload for a while, discard those observations, and only then start
recording.

*Coordinated omission.* Gil Tene's term for a subtler error. If a load
generator issues a request, waits for the response, and only then issues
the next, then a stall in the system under test also stalls the generator.
Requests that *would* have been sent during the stall, and would have
experienced it, are never sent, so they never appear in the data. The
measured distribution omits exactly the observations that would have shown
the problem, and it does so in coordination with the problem. The remedy
is to schedule requests by the clock, not by completion: if a request is
due at time t, its latency is measured from t, whether or not the previous
one has returned. The harness here does this. Foreground reads are due
every 500 ms and writes every 2 s on a fixed schedule; a slot that cannot
be issued because an admission limit was reached is counted as a *missed
slot*, and a missed slot is a failure.

## The real-process benchmark

The published numbers come from a harness under `scripts/benchmarks` that
measures the desktop chat notification consumer
([Chapter 20](20-desktop.qmd)) against everything below it.

**Real processes.** The Rust worker starts a real, isolated FOKS server and
a separate real agent process with private temporary client state and no
operating-system keyring. The Node side runs the *production* TypeScript
services (the inbox service, the notification consumer, and the
per-profile scheduler) against them. The measurement therefore covers the
service layer, the local IPC to the agent, the agent's own work, and the
network round trip to the server. It excludes rendering. Binaries are
release builds.

**Workloads and arms.** Four workloads, each run with notifications
`off` and `on`:

| Workload | Channels | Extra condition |
|---|---|---|
| steady | 70 | none |
| backlog | 70 | 120 sequentially confirmed sends injected at measurement start |
| wide | 200 | none |
| slow | 70 | 250 ms added after admission; one channel fails permanently |

A second account sends 6 incoming messages per second throughout.
Foreground history reads arrive every 500 ms and a foreground write
workflow every 2 s.

**Phases.** Each trial establishes baselines, then runs 15 s of warmup,
60 s of measurement, and a fixed 10 s drain during which no new traffic is
sent but in-flight sends remain in the denominator. The summarizer rejects
any trial whose phases are not exactly (15,000, 60,000, 10,000) ms as not
an acceptance result; shortened smoke runs are allowed for diagnosis but
cannot pass.

**Repetitions and ordering.** Three repetitions per arm, with arm order
alternated on each repetition so that neither arm systematically runs
first. Each completed trial is appended to a JSON-lines file and `fsync`ed;
the driver refuses to overwrite an existing results file.

**The metric.** Per trial, the p95 of successful foreground history
operations from submission to completion. The reported value per arm is
the **median of the three trial p95s**. Taking the median across trials
rather than pooling all observations means one anomalous trial (a
background process on the machine, say) cannot dominate, and it gives a
value that is itself an observation from a real trial rather than a
synthetic blend.

**The review trigger.** Notifications `on` versus `off` is flagged for
review if the p95 increase exceeds **both 20% and 50 ms**. Requiring both
avoids two false alarms: a 20% increase on a 10 ms baseline is 2 ms and
not worth a review, and a 50 ms increase on a 2 s baseline is noise. The
`slow` workload is exempt from the latency trigger because it exists to
verify that a permanent failure and an injected delay do not stop healthy
work.

**Correctness gates alongside latency.** A trial is not accepted on
percentiles alone. At least 99% of confirmed sends must be discovered by
the drain deadline; `lateDisplays` must be zero; all 120 foreground read
slots must have been issued; and concurrency observations must stay within
bounds (at most 2 jobs, 1 per profile, 1 background RPC).

**Provenance.** The driver records the SHA-256 of the agent binary, the
worker binary, the harness itself, every file under the desktop source
tree, and the shared limits file, plus the source revision and a digest of
any uncommitted patch, in every trial. A baseline mode extracts the
TypeScript from a fixed earlier commit while sharing the same native
binaries, so that only notification behavior differs between arms.
Event-loop delay is sampled at 20 ms and its p95 reported, so a
Node-side stall is distinguishable from an agent-side one.

### The published results

| Workload | Median of three trial p95s |
|---|---|
| Steady traffic, 70 channels | 43.7 ms |
| Message backlog, 70 channels | 38.4 ms |
| Steady traffic, 200 channels | 45.1 ms |

Linux x86_64, notifications on. The README's caption repeats the
conditions: 15 s warmup, 60 s measurement, 10 s drain, service/agent/server
path, rendering excluded. The benchmark guide adds the stance that recurs
throughout the repository's measurement notes: these are observations on
one machine, not product capacity claims.

## Scale tests

Two tests exist to exercise limits at their production size rather than at
the small sizes that keep an ordinary test suite fast.

**Notification rotation at 4,097 channels.** The notification consumer
bounds the number of per-channel progress records it keeps at 4,096 and
the number of channels it will evict per 5 s window at 64. The scale test
builds 17 stores totalling 4,097 channels, one more than the bound, and
asserts that exactly 64 evictions occur, that no state observation ever
exceeds 4,096 progress records or 64 queued, that no content pass runs
during pure rotation, and that after the 5 s window the rotation resumes.
The same function runs in the ordinary suite with the limits scaled to
16 and 4, and only with `FOKS_TEST_SCALE=1` at the production values.

**Incremental history at production page size.** The agent's incremental
history test runs at a page size of 3 in the ordinary suite so that page
boundaries, gaps, resets, and unknown channels are all reached quickly.
A second, ignored test runs the identical checks at the production page
size of 50 rows. Running the boundary logic at both sizes catches
off-by-one errors that only appear at one of them.

## One source of limits

Both of those tests depend on constants that must agree between Rust and
TypeScript. They live in a single JSON file,
`crates/foks-agent-proto/chat-limits.json`, compiled into Rust constants by
a build script and imported directly by the desktop's TypeScript.

| Constant | Value |
|---|---|
| `CHAT_PAGE_ROWS` | 50 |
| `CHAT_HISTORY_ROWS` | 1,000 |
| `CHAT_HISTORY_BYTES` | 8 MiB |
| `CHAT_INBOX_ROWS` | 1,000 |
| `CHAT_CHANNEL_ROWS` | 256 |
| `CHAT_TEXT_BYTES` | 65,536 |
| `CHAT_POLL_MILLISECONDS` | 55,000 |
| `CHAT_OPEN_VIEWS` | 32 |

The Rust agent asserts equality with its own copies in a test, and the
benchmark driver hashes the file into every trial's provenance, so a change
to a limit cannot go unrecorded.

## Measuring a stall: the checkpoint finding

Not every measurement is a percentile over a workload. Sometimes the
question is whether a specific mechanism causes a specific stall.
[Chapter 18](18-server-storage.qmd) described the choice of a `PASSIVE` WAL
checkpoint over `TRUNCATE`. The measurement behind it is a good example of
a small, targeted benchmark.

The comparison runs the real writer actor and the real maintenance code on
three disposable databases: `TRUNCATE` with unlimited WAL retention,
`PASSIVE` with unlimited retention, and `PASSIVE` with the proposed 16 MiB
reuse limit. It seeds 32 MiB of data while a read transaction is pinned,
then runs four phases with four concurrent writers and eight maintenance
passes: a reader held for the whole phase, catch-up after releasing it, two
overlapping short readers, and an online backup. Each run emits checkpoint
duration, SQLite's reported outcome and frame positions, and the writer
queue-wait distribution as p50, p95, p99, and maximum.

The finding was unambiguous in the held-reader phase: `TRUNCATE` produced
checkpoint maxima of 286 to 288 ms (a stall the benchmark deliberately
bounded with a 250 ms busy timeout; the production default is 5 s) and
queue p99 near 290 ms, while `PASSIVE` with the reuse limit produced
checkpoint maxima of 0.18 to 0.28 ms and queue p99 between 1 and 6 ms. The notes
also record what the measurement does *not* show: throughput ranges
between the two `PASSIVE` variants overlap, catch-up after the reader is
released still occupies the writer with maxima around 44 ms, and nothing
proves 16 MiB is the optimal limit. Three runs on one developer machine
are reported with their ranges, SQLite version, and build settings, and
the reader is asked to repeat them on representative storage before making
capacity claims.

## What good reporting looks like

The measurement notes across the repository share a few habits worth
adopting.

- Fixed durations and rates are inputs recorded with the result, never
  reconstructed afterward.
- Every reported number carries the hardware, build profile, and source
  revision it came from, and where possible the hashes of the binaries.
- Percentiles are reported with their sample counts, and the tail (p99 and
  maximum) is shown alongside the headline percentile.
- Correctness gates accompany latency gates; a fast failure is still a
  failure.
- The notes say what the measurement does not establish.
